lead: Location data is the phone's estimate of where it is: latitude, longitude and an accuracy radius. Location-based services (LBS) turn that stream of fixes into an answer — what is near me, did the user enter my zone, where is my rider, which offer fits this shop. Ride-hailing, food delivery and geofenced alerts all run on it. This chapter shows how Android gives an app location, and how the app uses it. Only a few universities teach this chapter.
prereq: You need: activities and the permission model from Unit 2, plus the tracking idea from Unit 1 (see Unit 1, Handover, location tracking and mobility management).

sections.h3: Fine versus coarse, and the providers

blocks.text: Android guards location because it reveals where a person lives and works. ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION gives accuracy to a few metres; ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION gives about a kilometre. Coarse suits weather or city-level offers; ask for fine only when a map pin or a 100 m geofence needs it. The manifest declaration alone is not enough on modern Android: the app must also request the permission at runtime and handle a refusal.
Below the permission sits a provider, the actual source of fixes.

items: GPS: satellites, accurate to metres outdoors, slow first fix, fails indoors, heavy on battery.
Network: Wi-Fi and cell-tower lookup, fast, works indoors, accuracy tens to hundreds of metres.
Passive: fixes other apps already requested, free, arrives unpredictably.

blocks.text: LocationManager is in the platform; you name the provider yourself. FusedLocationProviderClient, from Google Play services, merges GPS, Wi-Fi and sensors into one better fix. Both return a Location: latitude and longitude in degrees, accuracy in metres, and a time stamp.
getLastKnownLocation(provider) returns the last cached fix — possibly null, possibly minutes old — without waking any radio. Show it as a placeholder, then request live updates.

blocks.where: minTime is the minimum gap between fixes in milliseconds; minDistance is the minimum movement in metres before a new fix is delivered; listener is the LocationListener that receives each Location.

blocks.text: Both numbers are filters, not a schedule: the system may deliver later, never earlier. Stop with removeUpdates(listener) in onPause() and register again in onResume(); a paused activity that keeps GPS alive only drains the battery. The fused client uses requestLocationUpdates(request, callback, Looper) and removeLocationUpdates(callback), with the interval and displacement held in a LocationRequest.
Test every fix with getAccuracy(); 900 m is a city, not a doorstep. Throw away stale fixes by comparing getTime() with the current clock.

Geocoding maps an address to latitude and longitude; reverse geocoding maps coordinates to a street address. Geocoder returns lists and is slow, so call it off the main thread. addProximityAlert(latitude, longitude, radius, expiration, pendingIntent) fires an Intent when the device enters or leaves a circle of radius metres, and the Play services geofencing API does the same for many zones with less battery.
Typical services: nearby search for an ATM, tracking a delivery rider, a school-zone alert, a mall coupon when you walk in. To draw the fix on a map, see Chapter 5.2.

figure.caption: Each 20 s block, the rider at 5 m/s moves 5 × 20 = 100 m, exactly the minimum distance, so the time filter decides and fixes 1, 2 and 3 can arrive at the ticks. That gives at most 60 ÷ 20 = 3 updates in a minute.

spec.aria: A 60-second timeline: the rider moving at 5 metres per second covers 100 metres in each 20-second block, so the 100-metre distance filter is met and at most three fixes are delivered in a minute, marked 1, 2 and 3.

examples.question: A delivery app requests location updates every 20 s with a minimum distance of 100 m. A rider moves at 18 km/h. What is the maximum number of updates per minute, and how far does the rider move between two time ticks?
steps: Speed in metres per second: 18 km/h = 18000 m ÷ 3600 s = 5 m/s.
Distance moved in one 20 s tick: 5 m/s × 20 s = 100 m.
100 m is not less than the 100 m filter, so the distance filter is met at every tick; the time filter alone decides.
examples.answer: At most 3 updates per minute, with the rider moving exactly 100 m between ticks.
examples.check:
speed = 18 * 1000 / 3600
dist = speed * 20
updates = 60 / 20
print(speed)
print(dist)
print(updates)

traps: Manifest permission alone is not enough on modern Android; ask for fine or coarse location at runtime and handle a denial.
minTime is in milliseconds: 20 s must be written 20000, not 20.
minTime and minDistance are lower bounds. The system can deliver later, never earlier.
getLastKnownLocation can return null or a stale fix; it never wakes the GPS.
A user may grant only coarse even when you asked for fine; check the accuracy you actually received.

quiz.q: Name the three Android location providers and one property of each.
quiz.a: GPS: metres accurate outdoors, slow, battery heavy. Network: fast indoors, hundreds of metres. Passive: free, unpredictable.

quiz.q: Why ask for location at runtime when the manifest already declares the permission?
quiz.a: The manifest records intent only. The user grants at runtime, so a downloaded app cannot silently track; a refusal or a coarse-only grant must be handled.

quiz.q: Updates are requested every 30 s with a 50 m minimum distance. A user walks at 1.2 m/s. How many updates per minute at most?
quiz.a: In 30 s the user covers 1.2 × 30 = 36 m < 50 m, so no fix is delivered at the tick. 50 m takes 50 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 41.7 s, so at most one update per 41.7 s, about 1.4 per minute.

quiz.q: A tracking screen shows fixes with 800 m accuracy inside a city. Give two causes and two fixes.
quiz.a: Causes: only coarse permission granted, or the network provider used with no GPS view of the sky. Fixes: request fine permission and read the grant result; use the fused client at high accuracy and wait for an outdoor fix.

quiz.q: Give the difference between geocoding and reverse geocoding.
quiz.a: Geocoding turns an address into latitude and longitude. Reverse geocoding turns coordinates into an address. Both are slow, so run them off the main thread.
A paused activity cannot show fixes, but GPS keeps the radio and battery busy and the listener holds the activity; removing stops both.

beyond: Not for the exam. Indoors, GPS fails and Wi-Fi round-trip time plus Bluetooth beacons take over. Android now offers an approximate-location switch and treats background location as a separate, justified permission. Geofencing APIs batch many zones so the radio wakes rarely. Surveying uses RTK correction for centimetre fixes. Search for "Android location permissions", "FusedLocationProviderClient" and "geofencing API" next.
